podcast.title: Grammy Award for Liner Notes (1964)
podcast.body: The Grammy Award for Best Liner Notes, established in 1964, predominantly recognized classical recordings, along with collections, anthologies, or greatest hits packages. This trend continued for many years, highlighting the academic and informative nature of liner notes in the classical genre. "Pretty much every award has been given out to someone who has written liner notes for classical recordings, or a collection, or an anthology, or a great-a-titz package"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early CD Technology Showcases (1979-1982)
podcast.body: Classical music played a pivotal role in the early demonstration and commercialization of compact disc technology. The first test pressing in 1979 featured the Berlin Philharmonic performing Richard Strauss's "An Alpine Symphony," selected for its clarity and dynamic range. Later, Chopin's waltzes, performed by Claudia Arrau, became the first CD produced for public consumption on August 17, 1982. "The first test pressing, a CD used to demonstrate the new technology, was a recording of the Berlin Philharmonic, conducted by Herbert von Karrihan, performing Richard Strauss' and Elpine Symphony. This appeared in 1979, and this recording was chosen for its clarity and wide range of dynamics, something that the compact is promised."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

podcast.title: Early Adoption of Compact Disc (1981-1985)
podcast.body: Classical music aficionados and orchestra conductors, notably Herbert von Karajan, quickly embraced the Compact Disc in the early 1980s. This rapid adoption was due to the CD's ability to overcome inherent limitations of vinyl records, such as channel contamination and intrinsic noise, which significantly affected the clarity and fidelity of classical recordings. "Los grandes aficionados y directores Orquesta de la música clásica no eran unos grandes defensores del disco de vinilo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence on Wine Purchasing Behavior (1993)
podcast.body: A 1993 experiment demonstrated that playing classical music in a wine store influenced customer behavior. Shoppers would spend more time examining wine labels and were more likely to purchase more expensive bottles compared to when other genres of music were played. "A 1993 experiment showed that when classical music was played, people stopped and examined the labels more often and more carefully when compared to times when other genres of music were playing. They also ended up buying more expensive bottles of wine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition

podcast.title: EMI's Composition of Bach-Style Music (1997)
podcast.body: At a 1997 University of Oregon competition, the computer program EMI (Experiments in Musical Intelligence), developed by David Cope, composed pieces in the style of classical composer J.S. Bach. While music experts could discern it was computer-generated, they believed the program had played an actual Bach composition, demonstrating its sophisticated mimicry. "One was by a computer called EMI, which was given information on the musical style of classical composer J.S. Bach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History and Future of AI in Music

podcast.title: Crowd-Surfing Incident (2014)
podcast.body: In 2014, an audience member was ejected from a classical music concert for crowd-surfing during a performance of Handel's Messiah. This unusual incident highlighted how deeply ingrained and widespread crowd-surfing had become, even in genres traditionally associated with formal audience behavior. "In 2014, an audience member was ejected for crowd-serving during a classical music concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Faster Performance and Recording Tempo (2018 Study)
podcast.body: A 2018 study indicated that both live performances and studio recordings of classical music are now up to 30% faster than they were sixty years prior, suggesting a general acceleration in the genre's delivery. "A 2018 study says the classical music performances and recordings are up to 30% faster than they were 60 years ago."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 19th-Century Revival
podcast.body: After Johann Sebastian Bach's death in March 1685, he was nearly forgotten until a significant revival in the 19th century re-established him as a retro hero and one of the most important and influential composers of all time. "The only reason we talk about Bach today is because there was a Bach revival in the 19th century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Adam Jones' Musical Background
podcast.body: Adam Jones of Tool learned classical music through his violin training via the Suzuki method, an influence that can be heard in Tool's music. "and he learned to play classical music, which of course makes sense if you're at all familiar with Toul's music, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ancient Roots
podcast.body: Classical music dates back at least 600 years. "Classical music goes back at least 600 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Audio Testing
podcast.body: Classical music was among the various genres rigorously tested by Bernhard Grill during the development of the MP3 compression software. This extensive testing aimed to ensure the algorithm's effectiveness across a wide range of musical complexities. "He tried every form of music. Rock, metal, funk, jazz, classical, pop, everything but rap because he hated rap."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of the MP3

podcast.title: Carol of the Drum Composition
podcast.body: Catherine Davis, a classical composer, wrote "Carol of the Drum" in 1941, reportedly drawing inspiration from a Czech song that has never been definitively located. "In 1941, Catherine Davis, a classical composer, wrote Carol of the Drum, apparently loosely basing it on a check song that's never been found."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Composer Style for Johnny Greenwood
podcast.body: Johnny Greenwood works in full-on classical music styles as a composer for movie, TV, and documentary soundtracks. "This guy can work in a variety of styles. Rock, indie, jazz, chamber orchestra, and full-on classical music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comprehensive Music Classification
podcast.body: Classical music was acknowledged as a genre that couldn't be omitted from the comprehensive categorization of music, even in the context of popular music discussions from 1955. This underscores its distinct and enduring presence in the musical landscape. "And I guess we can't leave out classical can we?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continuous Use of Mutes
podcast.body: Mutes for brass and other instruments have been used for centuries and continue to be a standard practice in classical music performances. "They're still being used in classical music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discontent with Vinyl Records
podcast.body: Classical music enthusiasts and conductors were not strong advocates of vinyl records despite their wide frequency range. They found vinyl problematic due to issues like channel contamination, intrinsic noise, and complex processes that compromised the clarity of classical music. "Eran grandes enemigos de un gran desproblemas que tenía el disco de vinilo, sobre todo en la contaminación de canales, son el ruido intrínseco, en ciertos procesos un poco complejos, que afectaban bastante a la nicidez de la música clásica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Disliked by Psychopathic-Trending Individuals
podcast.body: A study conducted at New York University found that classical music was generally disliked by students who scored high on psychopathy scales. These individuals tended to rate classical pieces very low in preference. "same thing with classical music they didn't like it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition

podcast.title: Domain of Early Albums
podcast.body: Before the mid-1960s, albums were predominantly used for "adult music" genres such as classical, jazz, and Broadway show recordings. This perception shifted as rock music developed, producing sophisticated albums that garnered similar recognition. "Prior to the mid-1960s, albums had been the domain of adult music, serious music, jazz, classical, Broadway show recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Grammy Category
podcast.body: Classical music was one of the established Grammy award categories from the inception of the awards in 1959. "Jazz, classical, pop, country, Broadway, movie soundtracks, even comedy and children's music had Grammy award categories."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: And the Grammy Goes to… Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: And the Grammy Goes to… Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Early LP Domain (1950s)
podcast.body: In the early 1950s, classical music, along with jazz and Broadway show music, was considered "serious music" and was primarily found on 12-inch LPs. "serious music, which would be classical jazz, Broadway show music, was found on LPs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Liner Notes Context (Early 20th Century)
podcast.body: The tradition of adding explanatory text to recorded music packaging emerged in the first half of the 20th century, following the practice of printed music programs handed out at symphonies and operas. With the introduction of the 12-inch LP in 1948, which was initially reserved for genres like classical music, extensive essays were commissioned to educate listeners. "These were then sold together in a package that looked like a photo album, except that this was called a record album, and yes, that is the origin of the modern term."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Elvis Costello's Hybrid Album
podcast.body: Elvis Costello recorded a hybrid classical pop album, "The Juliet Letters," with the string players of The Brodsky Quartet. This project demonstrated his continuous refusal to be limited by genre and his exploration of new musical territories. "He has recorded a hybrid classical pop album with string players, The Brodsky Quartet."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Historical Perception in Late 19th/Early 20th Century
podcast.body: During the late 19th and early 20th century, classical music was regarded by elders as "uplifting and sophisticated," distinguishing it from popular genres that were often met with disdain.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Historical Use of Devil's Triad
podcast.body: The "devil's tri tone" (flattened fifth) was not exclusively found in modern music but also appeared in numerous classical compositions. Renowned composers such as Beethoven, Wagner, Debussy, Liszt, Sibelius, and Bartók all incorporated this dissonant interval into their works, demonstrating its long-standing presence in musical history. "But then it did show up in a lot of classical compositions from people like Beethoven, Wagner, Debussy, Lyst, Sabelius, Bartok, dozens of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: Historical Use of Vocables
podcast.body: Back in the 15th century, classical composers commonly used specific vocables as filler words in their songs. Thomas Morley's "Will You Buy a Fine Dog?" from the 1500s notably features "Dildo" repeatedly as a vocable. "Back in the 15th century, classical composers used a specific vocable as a filler word for songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: IMS's "Hello World" (N/A) – First Fully Computer-Composed Classical Piece
podcast.body: Engineers at the University of Melaga in Spain developed IMS, a program capable of generating new music based on analysis of existing compositions. IMS composed "Hello World," a classical piece for clarinet, violin, and piano, which is recognized as the first piece of music entirely conceived and notated by a computer without any human intervention. "IMS composed Hello World, the first piece of music completely created and notated without any kind of human intervention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History and Future of AI in Music

podcast.title: Joe Jackson's Teenage Dream
podcast.body: Joe Jackson fulfilled his original teenage dream of being a classical composer with his 1987 vocal-free LP "Will Power." While some critics found it pretentious, many were impressed by his ambitious foray into the genre, showcasing his wide musical range. "Jackson even tried fulfilling his original teenage dream of being a classical composer with 1987's Vocal Free LP Will Power."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Loiterer Deterrent
podcast.body: Classical music is used as a benign way to deter loiterers outside convenient stores. Playing it seems to effectively make people leave the area. "A more benign way of doing this is playing classical music. Let's say you have a convenient store. You don't want people hanging around outside. What do you do? You play classical music, and that seems to get rid of everybody."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long Hair as a Fashionable Choice
podcast.body: In earlier periods, it was entirely fashionable for eminent classical musicians like Beethoven and Mozart, as well as their contemporaries and successors, to wear long hair. This indicates a cyclical nature of fashion trends in men's hairstyles, where long hair was once a mark of distinction in classical music. "Now, that's a bit weird because not that much earlier, it was completely fashionable for the greatest classical musicians in the world to wear their hair long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manhattan Records' Focus
podcast.body: Classical music was one of the primary genres that Manhattan Records, a sister label to Blue Note, specialized in. "Manhattan Records, which was a sort of sister label to Blue Note that Bruce oversaw, which was either classical or musical theater kind of adult contemporary."

podcast.title: Matt Bellamy's Influence
podcast.body: Matt Bellamy incorporates classical elements into his guitar style, with noted similarities between some Muse songs and the works of composers like Chopin and Rachmaninoff. "And if you want to get really nerdy, you can find similarities between some mu songs and Chopin and Rockman enough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nazi Propaganda and Re-education
podcast.body: Starting in 1933 with the opening of the first concentration camp in Dachau, patriotic German music and German classical music and operas were used to re-educate inmates in the Nazi way and exemplify "good German values" for the general population. Anything experimental, or outside traditional structure, was banned. "At first, patriotic German music was used to re-educate inmates in the Nazi way... German classical music and operas exemplified good German values. Anything experimental that is something outside the traditional structure was banned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonders in Classical Music
podcast.body: Classical music also features its share of "one-hit wonders," composers largely known for a single, ubiquitous piece despite having created a vast body of work. Johann Pachelbel with "Canon in D" is a prime example, alongside figures like Jeremiah Clark, Samuel Barber, and Thomas Albinoni. "There's a whole subset of classical music fans devoted to these kinds of one hit wonders. They'll bring up names like Jeremiah Clark, Samuel Barner and Thomas Albionini."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Pain Control Application
podcast.body: Classical music is recommended as the best music for controlling pain if the individual suffering cannot control what music is played. Specifically, Mozart, combined with Advil, has been proven to effectively work on inflammation. "if the person can't be in charge, go with classical music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: Palestinian Detainee Torture
podcast.body: Reports from Israel indicated that Palestinian detainees were tied to tiny chairs with hoods over their heads and blasted with classical music at high volume as a form of interrogation and torture. "Also from Israel, there were reports of Palestinian detainees being tied to tiny chairs with hoods over their heads and blasted with classical music at high volume."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pet Preference (Cats)
podcast.body: Research conducted at Louisiana State University indicates that cats have a strong preference for classical music. "Cats love classical music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: RCA's Red and Midnight Blue Vinyl Coding
podcast.body: RCA assigned red vinyl for "serious classical" music and midnight blue for "popular classical" releases as part of its short-lived color-coding system for 7-inch singles. "Serious classical was red. Popular classical was midnight blue."

podcast.title: Scatological Humor in the 18th Century
podcast.body: The presence of scatological humor in the works and letters of classical composers like Mozart demonstrates that such humor was more mainstream and accepted in polite society in the 18th century than it is today. "it reinforces the thinking that scatter logical humor was way more mainstream back then, including in polite society than it is today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seeking Complexity with Age
podcast.body: With increasing age, individuals may turn to classical music in their pursuit of "complexity, challenge and sophistication" in their listening habits. This indicates an evolving relationship with music, moving beyond earlier identity-driven preferences.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Shift from LP Domain (1960s)
podcast.body: By the 1960s, LPs were no longer exclusively the domain of serious music like classical, as rock and pop music began to be collected on albums. "LPs were no longer the domain of good or serious music like classical or jazz or movie soundtracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Studying Aid for High Achievers
podcast.body: Classical music was identified as the number one genre listened to by students who achieved the highest grades, suggesting it is highly effective for studying. "Number one, classical."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Survey Says: Useful and Odd Music Surveys and Polls

podcast.title: The Mozart Effect Controversy
podcast.body: Classical music became central to the "Mozart effect" theory, which proposed it could enhance infant intellect. This led to state-funded initiatives like Georgia providing classical music CDs to newborns. However, later research challenged the exclusivity of classical music's benefits, suggesting other forms of stimulation yielded similar results.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Traditional Album Format
podcast.body: Before 1965, albums were primarily reserved for "proper music" like classical recordings, jazz, soundtracks, and Broadway cast recordings, distinguishing them from the singles-driven pop and rock and roll markets.
